aspirin-mask.summary: A crushed-aspirin paste applied to the face to calm redness and breakouts, based on aspirin's chemical relation to salicylic acid.

quick.overview:
The aspirin mask is a home paste made from crushed aspirin tablets, applied to the face by people who want clearer, less red skin and fewer breakouts.

The reasoning runs through salicylic acid, a common acne ingredient: aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid and is broken down to salicylic acid in the body. Users expect a similar pore-clearing, calming effect on the skin. Salicylic acid itself is studied for acne; no studies of the aspirin mask were found.
quick.how: People mix crushed tablets with water or another base into a paste, leave it on for a short time as a wash-off mask, and rinse. It is used as an occasional spot or whole-face treatment alongside a normal cleanser and moisturizer. Users usually look for a change in redness within hours and in breakouts over repeated uses.
quick.risks: The documented warnings about aspirin concern oral use, such as stomach irritation and bleeding risk and avoidance by people with aspirin allergy. Effects of a topical aspirin paste are not described in the sources reviewed, so irritation on the face is possible but not characterised. People allergic to aspirin or salicylates have reason to avoid it.

angle.text: Users crush aspirin into a paste and apply it to the face for clearer, less red skin, reasoning from aspirin's relation to salicylic acid. Salicylic acid itself is studied for acne; the aspirin mask has not been.

honey-mask-manuka.summary: Manuka honey used as a wash-off face mask to calm skin and clear breakouts, drawing on honey's antibacterial and wound-care record.

quick.overview:
A manuka honey mask is honey from the manuka tree spread on the face and rinsed off, used to calm irritated skin and clear breakouts for a clearer, calmer complexion.

Proponents point to methylglyoxal, the compound credited for manuka's activity, and to antibacterial effects seen in lab studies. Honey has been studied in wound care, including early evidence of faster healing of partial-thickness burns. No acne studies were found.
quick.how: People apply a thin layer of manuka honey to clean skin, leave it on for a short period, and rinse with warm water, often once or a few times a week. It is used on its own or as part of a gentle routine. Users usually judge it by how calm and clear skin looks over a few weeks.
quick.risks: Honey is generally safe in food amounts, and honey is advised against for babies. Labelling and authenticity of manuka products are disputed, and grading systems such as UMF and MGO vary. As with any food product on skin, allergic reactions or irritation are possible in people sensitive to honey or bee products.

angle.text: Skincare fans apply manuka honey as a rinse-off mask to calm skin and clear breakouts, citing its antibacterial activity. Honey has been studied in wound care; no acne studies were found.

bentonite-clay-mask.summary: A wash-off clay mask that soaks up surface oil for a matte, less congested-looking face, popular with oily skin.

quick.overview:
A bentonite mask is a rinse-off paste made from an absorbent volcanic-ash clay. People with oily or congested skin use it to soak up surface oil and get a less shiny, cleaner-looking face.

Bentonite particles are flat with a large surface area and swell in water, so they adsorb liquids and oils. Users attribute the mattifying effect to this, and it lasts until sebum returns. The clay is a well-characterised industrial material, but no clinical trials of clay masks for oil control or acne were found.
quick.how: People mix the clay with water (sometimes with other liquids) into a paste, apply a layer to the face or body, leave it on until it begins to dry, and rinse off. It is typically used once or a few times a week within a routine that includes moisturizer afterward. The matte effect is visible straight after rinsing.
quick.risks: Bentonite is described as meeting FDA standards for contact with food and drugs, though the FDA has warned about at least one retail bentonite clay product. Clay can leave skin feeling dry or tight, and individual products and skin reactions vary.

angle.text: People with oily or congested skin use wash-off bentonite clay masks to soak up surface oil, leaving a matte, cleaner-looking face. The effect comes from the clay's absorbency; no clinical trials of clay masks were found.

vitamin-b5-pantothenic-acid-high-dose.summary: Very high-dose vitamin B5 taken in the hope of reducing skin oil and breakouts; no acne trials were found.

quick.overview:
Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) is an essential, over-the-counter vitamin. Some skincare and looksmaxxing posters take very large amounts hoping for less skin oil and fewer breakouts.

B5 is needed to make coenzyme A, which takes part in fatty acid metabolism, and proponents reason that this link could affect sebum. No clinical studies of high-dose B5 for acne or sebum were found, and the reference sources consulted do not discuss acne.
quick.how: It is taken as an oral supplement, usually as a standalone capsule or powder added to an existing supplement stack, for several weeks before users judge changes in skin oiliness. Some pair it with a normal cleanser and moisturizer routine.
quick.risks: No tolerable upper intake level has been set by US or European authorities because no harm from high intakes has been documented in humans. Some community members describe breakouts of their own while taking it; no published studies were identified on this.

angle.text: Skincare and looksmaxxing posters take very high-dose vitamin B5 hoping to reduce skin oil and breakouts. The theory draws on B5's role in fatty acid metabolism; no acne trials were found.

probiotics-for-acne.summary: Oral or topical probiotics used for fewer breakouts via the gut-skin axis and skin microbiome; reviews and trials exist and results vary by strain.

quick.overview:
Probiotics are live bacteria sold as capsules, fermented foods and skin products. Acne-prone people use them hoping for less inflammation and fewer breakouts.

The proposed routes are the gut-skin axis, where gut microbes influence inflammation and hormones, and shifts in skin bacteria such as C. acnes. A lab study found skin S. epidermidis can inhibit C. acnes through fermentation. Several meta-analyses of randomised trials appeared in 2025, and reviews describe the findings as preliminary, with early signs of fewer inflammatory lesions and better skin barrier function.
quick.how: People take oral probiotic capsules or eat fermented foods daily, or apply topical products to the face, usually alongside a regular skincare routine. Benefits reported in studies are strain-specific, so results do not carry over between products. Users typically allow several weeks before judging skin.
quick.risks: Probiotics are generally considered safe, but rare bloodstream infections have occurred in immunocompromised or critically ill people, who have reason to avoid them. Effects depend on the strain, and regulators such as EFSA have rejected probiotic health claims for insufficient evidence.

angle.text: Acne-prone users take oral probiotics or use topical ones to shift gut or skin microbes, lowering inflammation and breakouts. Reviews and trials exist, with results that vary by strain.

dim-supplement.summary: A broccoli-derived supplement used off-label to shift estrogen metabolism for fewer hormonal breakouts; its research is on hormones and cancer.

quick.overview:
DIM (3,3'-diindolylmethane) is formed when the body digests indole-3-carbinol from cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli and cabbage, and is sold as a supplement. In acne communities it is used for clearer skin by people with hormonal breakouts.

The idea is that DIM shifts estrogen metabolism and androgen balance, lowering androgen-driven oil. Lab studies report antiestrogenic activity through the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and altered sex hormone metabolism. Human research has focused on cancer and other conditions; no clinical studies of DIM for acne were found.
quick.how: It is taken as a daily oral capsule, often by people whose breakouts follow a hormonal pattern such as along the jawline or around the menstrual cycle. Users generally wait several weeks to a few months before judging skin changes.
quick.risks: Pure DIM carries skin, eye and respiratory irritation hazard labelling. Because it acts on hormone metabolism, people with hormone-sensitive conditions or who take hormonal medication have reason to check with a clinician first. Long-term effects of supplementation for acne have not been studied in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Used off-label for hormonal acne, DIM is taken to shift estrogen and androgen balance, lowering oil and breakouts. The research on DIM concerns hormones and cancer; acne has not been studied.

hypochlorous-acid-spray.summary: A mild antimicrobial mist, the same chemical white blood cells make, used on face and body for calmer, clearer-looking skin.

quick.overview:
A hypochlorous acid (HOCl) spray is a mild antimicrobial mist used on skin. HOCl is the same chemical neutrophils make to kill microbes. Acne-prone users spray it to reduce bacteria and soothe irritation for calmer, clearer-looking skin.

HOCl oxidises microbial proteins and damages membranes. In one study, an HOCl eyelid solution cut staphylococci by over 99% in 20 minutes. Since 2016 the US FDA has cleared products with HOCl as the main active for wounds and infections. No studies of cosmetic outcomes such as acne were identified.
quick.how: People mist it onto cleansed skin, or onto the chest and back, once or twice a day, often after workouts or shaving and before moisturizer. It is used as a gentle add-on to an existing routine and is also common after procedures such as microneedling.
quick.risks: The EPA classes it as non-hazardous, though as an oxidiser it can irritate depending on concentration. Solutions degrade and lose potency with time, heat and light, so shelf life is short.

angle.text: Acne-prone users mist hypochlorous acid on face or body to reduce bacteria and soothe irritation, for calmer, clearer-looking skin. It has regulatory clearance and studies in wound and eyelid care.

accure-laser-1726-nm.summary: An in-office 1726 nm laser that targets oil glands to reduce sebum and breakouts in persistent acne.

quick.overview:
Accure is a clinic laser using a 1726 nm wavelength that targets sebaceous (oil) glands. The payoff people want is less oil production and fewer breakouts in persistent acne, similar to Aviclear.

The wavelength is described as selective for sebaceous glands, aiming at oil production rather than the whole skin surface. Trial registrations show a completed 104-participant device study for acne and a 30-participant laser study, though outcomes are not reported in the registry entries.
quick.how: It is performed by clinicians in a series of in-office sessions spaced over weeks, usually by people whose acne has persisted despite other approaches. Results are judged over the following months as oil production changes.
quick.risks: Side effects were not reported in the sources reviewed. Cost and availability vary by clinic, and the treatment is only offered in clinical settings.

angle.text: Accure is an in-office 1726 nm laser used to shrink the oil glands behind persistent acne, so there is less sebum and fewer breakouts. Registered trials exist, with outcomes not yet reported in the registry entries.

isolaz-pulsed-light-acne-treatment.summary: A clinic treatment combining suction and pulsed light to clear clogged pores and calm acne-prone skin.

quick.overview:
Isolaz is an in-office device that pairs suction on the skin with pulses of broad-spectrum light. It is offered for clogged pores and acne, with the goal of clearer, smoother skin.

Intense pulsed light is absorbed by pigment, blood and water in the skin, and proponents say the vacuum component helps clear pores. General acne references describe light and laser therapies as add-on options used because of cost and limited evidence, not first-line care. Published information on the vacuum-assisted device specifically is thin.
quick.how: A clinician moves the handpiece over the face in a session, and treatment is typically repeated as a series, often alongside topical acne care. Results depend on skin tone and the practitioner.
quick.risks: Reported IPL complications include hyperpigmentation, with darker skin tones carrying more pigmentation risk. Certain medications and skin conditions are contraindications, so clinics screen for them.

angle.text: Isolaz is a clinic treatment combining suction and pulsed light, used to clear clogged pores and reduce congestion for clearer, smoother skin. Public information on the device itself is limited.

sun-exposure-for-acne.summary: Tanning or sitting in the sun to dry out blemishes and mask redness for a short-term evener look.

quick.overview:
Some people tan or sunbathe hoping to dry out blemishes. The payoff reported is a short-term improvement in how skin looks, as a tan can mask redness and make spots less obvious.

Proponents say UV makes blemishes look drier and less red. General acne references state sunlight exposure is not associated with acne overall, and that sun exposure can prolong post-acne dark marks (postinflammatory hyperpigmentation). No published trial supports sun as an acne treatment.
quick.how: People spend time in direct sun or use tanning, often in a series of sessions, and judge the result by how their complexion looks while tanned. Any improvement described is temporary.
quick.risks: UV can sustain postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, and intense UVA can trigger a separate eruption called acne aestivalis. Sun exposure carries general skin-damage and skin-cancer risk, and references advise daily sunscreen.

angle.text: Some people sit in the sun or tan to dry out blemishes and mask redness, reporting a short-term evener look. Reference sources link sun exposure to lingering dark marks.

face-touching-phone-hygiene-habit.summary: Wiping phones, changing pillowcases and keeping hands off the face to cut oil, dirt and friction on acne-prone skin.

quick.overview:
This is a low-effort routine of wiping phones, washing pillowcases and keeping hands off the face. People use it to reduce breakouts and keep skin clearer.

The idea is that it limits bacteria, oil and dirt transfer to skin and reduces friction. General acne references note that mechanical pressure from helmets or chinstraps can worsen existing acne (acne mechanica); they do not address phones or pillowcases specifically, and no studies test these habits directly.
quick.how: People wipe their phone screens regularly, change pillowcases on a set schedule, use a clean towel and avoid resting hands or phone against the face. It is combined with a normal cleanser and moisturizer routine, and users judge results over several weeks.
quick.risks: No specific risks are documented. References say washing affected skin more than twice daily is generally not recommended, so extra cleaning of the face itself is not part of the advice.

angle.text: Skincare communities wipe phones, wash pillowcases and keep hands off the face to cut bacteria, oil and friction on skin, aiming for fewer clogged pores and clearer-looking skin. Its effect on acne has not been tested directly.

minimalist-routine-gentle-cleanser-moist.summary: A pared-back routine of gentle cleanser plus moisturizer that keeps the skin barrier intact for calmer, clearer-looking skin.

quick.overview:
A minimalist routine strips skincare down to a gentle cleanser and a moisturizer. People use it to avoid irritating the skin barrier and to get calmer, less breakout-prone skin.

General dermatology guidance recommends non-comedogenic, oil-free products, moisturizing even for oily acne-prone skin because barrier dysfunction may contribute to acne, and limiting washing to no more than twice daily. A fragrance-free moisturizer may reduce irritation, and in one cited study a ceramide cleanser and cream were well tolerated alongside acne medication and improved adherence.
quick.how: People wash morning and evening with a mild non-foaming or low-foaming cleanser and follow with a moisturizer, dropping harsher exfoliants and multi-step products. It is also used as a base while on acne medication. Calmer skin is typically noticed over a few weeks.
quick.risks: No specific risks are documented. The routine does not itself treat acne, so people with persistent breakouts often add treatment on top.

angle.text: Users strip their routine to a gentle cleanser and moisturizer to protect the skin barrier, so skin stays calmer and less irritated. The approach matches general dermatology guidance on the barrier and moisturizing.

silicone-onion-extract-scar-gel-mederma.summary: Over-the-counter scar gels and silicone sheets used to make scars look softer, flatter and less noticeable.

quick.overview:
Mederma is a popular over-the-counter gel built around onion bulb extract, and silicone gels and sheets are a related class. People apply them to healed scars, including acne and surgical scars, hoping for softer, flatter, less noticeable scar tissue.

Two trials found the onion extract gel no better than petrolatum, and a rabbit ear study found improved collagen organization without significant reduction in scar size, height or inflammation. Silicone products have a larger body of scar research behind them.
quick.how: People rub the gel into a healed scar one to a few times a day, or wear silicone sheets over it, for weeks to months. It is used on the face, body and surgical scars once the wound has closed.
quick.risks: Safety data are limited in the sources reviewed. The Mederma product contains alcohol and fragrance, which can irritate sensitive skin.

angle.text: Mederma and silicone gels or sheets are applied to healed scars, including acne and surgical scars, to soften and flatten the tissue so scars look less noticeable. Trials of the onion extract gel found results similar to petrolatum, while silicone has more scar research.

subcision.summary: A clinic needle procedure that releases the bands pulling down rolling scars so the skin surface lifts and smooths.

quick.overview:
Subcision is a minor procedure in which a needle is inserted beneath the skin to cut the fibrous bands tethering a depressed scar, most often rolling acne scars. The payoff is a smoother skin surface as the scar lifts.

Releasing the scar creates a pocket where blood collects and collagen forms, which proponents say raises the scar. The term was coined in a 1995 paper describing a tri-beveled hypodermic needle. Studies include case series and small trials, and reviews list it within multimodal acne scar treatment.
quick.how: A clinician numbs the area and works the needle beneath each scarred zone, often in a series of sessions and combined with other scar treatments such as lasers or microneedling. Swelling and bruising settle over days, and collagen-related improvement is judged over following weeks to months.
quick.risks: Procedure-specific risks are not detailed in the sources reviewed, though bruising and swelling are expected from needle work under the skin. Medical sources describe subcision as in-office; do-it-yourself versions circulate in forums, where claims about results are anecdotal.

angle.text: Subcision is a clinic procedure that releases the fibrous bands pulling down rolling acne scars, so they lift and the skin surface looks smoother. Evidence consists of case series and small trials.

tca-cross.summary: Dermatologist-applied dabs of high-strength acid into icepick scars to rebuild collagen and make them shallower; small trials report improvement.

quick.overview:
TCA CROSS (chemical reconstruction of skin scars) is a dermatology procedure in which a clinician applies a high concentration of trichloroacetic acid to the base of individual atrophic acne scars, most often narrow icepick scars, rather than peeling the whole face. The payoff is shallower scars and smoother-looking skin.

The acid causes a controlled injury in the dermis, which authors propose triggers new collagen formation and lifts the scar floor. Published studies, mostly small and many without a control group, report meaningful improvement after a series of sessions, including in darker skin types. Comparisons against subcision, microneedling and pinpoint CO2 laser have been mixed.
quick.how: A clinician dabs the acid into each scar and repeats sessions every few weeks, with studies using concentrations from 50% to 100%. It is often combined with other scar treatments. Improvement is judged over the weeks and months after a series.
quick.risks: The original authors reported no significant complications in a 65-patient series. Acid at these strengths is not an over-the-counter product and the procedure is clinician-performed. Trials are small and mostly open-label.

angle.text: TCA CROSS is used by dermatologists to make narrow, deep icepick acne scars shallower by applying strong acid to individual scars, prompting collagen to rebuild in the pit. Small trials report improvement, including in darker skin types.

punch-excision-punch-elevation.summary: Minor surgery that cuts out or lifts individual deep acne scars with a small punch tool so skin sits level and looks smoother.

quick.overview:
Punch excision and punch elevation are minor surgical techniques for atrophic acne scars, particularly deep boxcar scars with sharp edges. The payoff is smoother-looking cheeks where deep pits are removed or raised level with the surrounding skin.

In punch excision, a small circular blade removes the scar and the wound is closed; in punch elevation, the scar base is cut free and raised level with the skin. Both were named in a widely cited 2001 review proposing the icepick, rolling and boxcar scar classification. Randomised trials identifying a best method are limited, and a 2024 review notes combining treatments would likely produce more benefit than a single method.
quick.how: A clinician performs the procedure under local anaesthetic, often scar by scar. It is usually followed by resurfacing such as lasers or dermabrasion to blend the treated area, with healing over days to weeks.
quick.risks: As surgical procedures they carry the general risks of skin surgery, including a residual or new scar, infection and pigment change. Reviews describe them as clinician-performed and as part of combined approaches.

angle.text: Punch excision and elevation are used on deep boxcar acne scars, either removing the scar or raising its base to skin level for a smoother-looking surface. The techniques are long established in dermatology, with limited trial-level data.

phenol-baker-gordon-peel.summary: The deepest classic chemical peel, resurfacing coarse wrinkles, sun damage and some scarring, performed under medical supervision.

quick.overview:
The Baker-Gordon peel is a deep chemical peel based on phenol and croton oil, introduced in the early 1960s. It is used for deep wrinkles, sun damage and some scarring, and is regarded in the medical literature as the strongest of the traditional peels.

Phenol destroys the outer skin layers and croton oil is described as increasing penetration. The skin then regenerates over days to weeks with new collagen, giving fewer wrinkles and smoother texture. Phenol-croton oil peels were used discreetly by early Hollywood stars in the 1920s and entered mainstream practice in the 1960s. No clinical trials were located; the information comes from encyclopedic summaries.
quick.how: It is performed under medical supervision with sedation or anaesthesia and cardiac monitoring, usually as a single treatment per area, followed by a long recovery. In looksmaxxing discussions it is a rare, high-stakes procedure.
quick.risks: Reported risks include heart rhythm disturbances from systemic phenol absorption, permanent lightening of skin (hypopigmentation), scarring, infection and herpes reactivation. Wikipedia notes that the deeper the peel, the more complications can arise.

angle.text: The phenol or Baker-Gordon peel is the deepest classic chemical peel, causing a controlled deep injury so skin regenerates with new collagen, for fewer wrinkles and smoother texture. It is performed under medical supervision, and its results are documented mainly in older clinical reports.

prp-microneedling-vampire-facial.summary: Microneedling with a layer of your own platelet-rich plasma, offered for smoother skin and softer acne scars.

quick.overview:
PRP microneedling, marketed as the vampire facial, combines microneedling with platelet-rich plasma prepared from the client's own blood. It is offered for skin texture, acne scars and general rejuvenation, and gained attention through celebrity endorsement in the 2010s.

Blood is spun in a centrifuge to concentrate platelets, which carry growth factors, and the plasma is applied during or after microneedling. Proponents say the growth factors boost healing and collagen production. Studies of microneedling are mostly small, and Wikipedia describes the added efficacy of PRP as in question pending scientific studies. On looksmax.org, users post before-and-after accounts and discuss DIY variants such as PRP creams.
quick.how: A clinic draws blood, processes it, and applies the plasma while a microneedling device makes tiny punctures in the skin. It is typically done as a series of sessions spaced weeks apart, with redness and swelling for a few days afterward.
quick.risks: The main concern raised in sources is infection when procedures are done in non-medical settings with poor infection control. In April 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses among patients of an unlicensed Albuquerque spa; about 200 other clients and partners tested negative. PRP is exempt from FDA regulation as a product, while the preparation devices need clearance.

angle.text: The vampire facial pairs microneedling with a person's own platelet-rich plasma to remodel collagen for smoother skin and softer acne scars. Microneedling itself is studied for scars, while the added benefit of PRP is in question pending studies.

exosome-treatments.summary: Stem-cell-derived vesicle serums applied after microneedling for fresher, smoother-looking skin, scars and hair.

quick.overview:
Exosomes are tiny membrane-bound vesicles released by cells. Cosmetic products marketed as exosome serums use vesicles from sources such as stem cells, applied after microneedling for rejuvenation, scars, under-eye concerns and hair.

Exosomes carry proteins, lipids and nucleic acids between cells, and proponents propose these cargoes can signal skin cells to repair, giving fresher, smoother-looking skin. Laboratory research on exosomes is extensive, but Wikipedia describes limited definitive evidence of functional transfer in humans. Registered clinical trials in skin aging and hair loss are early-stage or have ended without results being listed.
quick.how: A clinician applies the serum to skin right after microneedling, usually as part of a series of sessions. Users look for gradual changes in texture and tone over following weeks.
quick.risks: In late 2019 the FDA issued an advisory about noncompliant exosome marketing and patient injuries linked to exosome injections, stating that exosomes are drug products requiring pre-market approval. Wikipedia describes ongoing unapproved marketing of cosmetic exosome products. Products differ in source and purity.

angle.text: Exosome serums are applied after microneedling to signal skin cells to repair, aiming for fresher, smoother skin, softer scars and hair support. Exosome biology is well studied in labs, while cosmetic use on skin has few small trials.

picosecond-laser-picosure-picoway.summary: Ultra-short-pulse clinic laser used to break up pigment and tattoos and smooth acne scars and skin texture.

quick.overview:
Picosecond lasers deliver energy in trillionths of a second. PicoSure and PicoWay are commercial devices of this type, used in clinics for pigment, tattoos, skin texture and acne scars, aiming for smoother, more even skin.

A fractionated picosecond laser creates tiny zones of injury in the epidermis; a microscopy study in one volunteer found micro-injuries concentrated in pigmented cells, with debris exfoliated over about four weeks. A 2020 study of 18 completers reported improvement in scar scores after six sessions. Registered trials also cover wrinkles, melasma and skin tightening.
quick.how: Treatments are done in clinics as a series of sessions spaced weeks apart. Users judge results by pigment and scar appearance over the following months.
quick.risks: The 2020 acne scar study concluded the treatment was safe in 18 patients with skin types III-IV; no large safety dataset was identified, and pain was measured as an outcome. Results in other skin types are not covered, and the procedure is performed in clinics.

angle.text: Picosecond lasers are used in clinics to break up pigment and stimulate collagen for smoother, more even skin and softer acne scars. Small prospective studies report scar improvement.
